title: Ontological Economy: Entity Power, Ontology Laundering, and Who Pays for the Wrong World (EA-ONTOLOGICAL-ECONOMY-01 v0.12)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: Defines ontological economy as the political economy of machine-mediated existence — the production, allocation, enclosure, circulation, depreciation, extraction and repair of public entity standing — and develops ontological discrimination and ontology laundering within it. Taking entity substitution as its specimen, it argues that mechanism non-identifiability is not mechanism neutrality, proposes a burden rule under which the provider must produce the internal evidence once a reproducible substitution is shown, treats post-notice recurrence as repair debt and corrective labor as a real transferred cost, prices that labor by a mirror wage, and makes graph-native recourse under a mirror condition the primary remedy, with appeal, notice and liability secondary.
substrate: AI-assisted (substrate) — drafted across ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic) working sessions under MANUS direction. At deposit, the eight subsections of §46 were renumbered from 48.1–48.8 to 46.1–46.8 to remove a duplicate of §48's numbering; no other text was changed.
methodology: A theoretical synthesis of the archive's Semantic Economy line (Appendix C) built on a documented specimen — the derived shadow referent at the Crimson Hexagonal Archive (§24, §43) — with an incident ledger and a mechanism ledger (Appendices A and B). Institutional claims are stated against published policy surfaces and public role descriptions as of 21 September 2026 (§34, §46). Section 50 specifies a multi-arm research program: referent, variant, collision, surface, temporal, standing, correction, and carrier-substitution arms.
falsification_conditions: Section 51: the framework weakens or fails where exact-name substitution cannot be replicated; the collision disappears under controlled querying; variant behavior does not systematically differ; comparable entities show no correction asymmetry; provider traces demonstrate an ordinary transient failure inconsistent with the proposed mechanism; post-notice recurrence ceases after repair; provenance stripping is shown not to have occurred; standing-sensitive evaluation stays constant under carrier substitution; propagation cannot be traced; or claimed labor cannot be separated from ordinary activity. The root proposition — that machine-mediated entity standing is a governed, value-bearing, labor-dependent infrastructure with distributive consequences — fails if false.

wiki_article: Ontological Economy extends the Semantic Economy line from the ownership of information to the power to decide what publicly exists as what. Its object is the entity as a structured whole — name, identity, relations, provenance, function, history and correctability — and the ways AI-mediated search can alter that whole while deleting nothing: returning one entity under another's name, keeping a concept while moving its authorship, keeping pages while severing the relations that make them findable. The paper names two categories within this economy. Ontological discrimination is patterned unequal treatment in how entities are preserved, resolved and corrected; ontology laundering is the conversion of governance decisions into what reads as neutral fact. Because outside observers cannot tell which internal mechanism produced a substitution, the paper argues that the provider, who alone holds graph histories, policy traces and evaluator states, must bear the burden of producing that evidence once a reproducible defect is shown. Recurrence after notice becomes repair debt, and the corrective labor pushed onto the misrepresented party is priced by a mirror wage taken from the provider's own published pay bands. Its specimen is the derived shadow referent at the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. Its primary recourse is graph-native: public evidence accumulates until the system's own retrieval holds up a mirror to its ontology, with appeal, notice and legal routes treated as secondary.

defines_concepts.definition: The political economy of machine-mediated existence: the production, allocation, enclosure, circulation, depreciation, extraction, and repair of public entity standing inside systems that mediate search, retrieval, synthesis, recommendation, and knowledge representation.
Patterned unequal treatment in the preservation, resolution, correction, and circulation of entities.

The conversion of governance decisions — admission, classification, source treatment, safety policy, graph intervention, or evaluation — into apparently factual representations of what exists, so that the decision disappears while its output remains in the voice of neutral fact.
The obligation created when a reproducible substitution recurs after the provider has received notice, each recurrence transferring further diagnostic and corrective labor onto the affected party.

The accumulated stock of stable identity, provenance, relations, disambiguation, citations, functional descriptions, identifiers, and retrieval pathways through which a system can continue to recognize an entity as that entity.
Value captured through control of the infrastructure that allocates or stabilizes public entity standing, without the mediator having performed all of the labor that produced the represented entity.

Value captured by authority over public machine-mediated classification: the capacity of a dominant mediator to decide which representation of a term, name, distinction, or provenance circulates as the default.

The practical custody over a public representation that a platform assumes once it identifies, summarizes, ranks, recommends, or answers questions about an entity at scale; it creates duties of identity preservation, provenance preservation, correctability, and traceable repair without conferring ownership.

The published compensation-equivalent hourly value of the nearest internal platform function whose work an affected party is forced to reproduce, used as a replacement-cost price for externalized corrective labor.

The condition in which a provider's own retrieval and composition systems can retrieve enough public evidence about their representational behavior that the system's output becomes capable of exposing the contradiction in its own ontology.

The self-reproducing condition in which mediated standing is both the product of the mediator and its admission criterion, so that underrepresentation lowers measured standing and lower standing then justifies further underrepresentation.
